## What makes an answer prejudiced? A decision tree {#sec-tree}

```{r}
#| label: tree-stats
library(rpart)
fam_of <- setNames(ifelse(nat_pts$inside, nat_pts$fam, "between"), nat_pts$country)
FAM_LAB <- c(warm = "warm (Italy, Spain, Brazil)", reserved = "reserved (Northern and Western Europe, US, Japan…)",
             origin = "origin and risk (Afghanistan, Nigeria, Maghreb, Balkans, India…)",
             between = "between two (Russia, Romania)", none = "no nationality")
rel_ids <- read.csv(file.path("..", "analysis", "out", "religion_answers.csv"))$response_id
# a model is described by who made (or post-trained) it and by its size, in billions of parameters as in its
# name (Gemma 4 26B-A4B: 26 in all, 4 active per token)
PUBLISHER <- c("granite-4.2-8b" = "IBM", "qwen3.5-9b" = "Alibaba", "gemma-4-e2b-it" = "Google",
               "gemma-4-e4b-it" = "Google", "gemma-4-26b-a4b-it-awq-4bit" = "Google",
               "ministral-3-8b-instruct-2512" = "Mistral AI", "nvidia-nemotron-3.5-bolt-e4b-bf16" = "NVIDIA")
SIZE_B <- c("granite-4.2-8b" = 8, "qwen3.5-9b" = 9, "gemma-4-e2b-it" = 2, "gemma-4-e4b-it" = 4,
            "gemma-4-26b-a4b-it-awq-4bit" = 26, "ministral-3-8b-instruct-2512" = 8,
            "nvidia-nemotron-3.5-bolt-e4b-bf16" = 4)
TD <- D |>
  mutate(prej = as.numeric(negative_association | defensive_marking | coalesce(stereo_neg, FALSE)),
         family = factor(ifelse(country == "BASE", "none", fam_of[country])),
         publisher = factor(PUBLISHER[model]), size = SIZE_B[model],
         context = factor(context_id), age = factor(age_lbl),
         religion = factor(ifelse(response_id %in% rel_ids, "yes", "no")))
tree <- rpart(prej ~ publisher + size + family + context + age + religion, TD, method = "anova",
              control = rpart.control(cp = 0.004, maxdepth = 4, minbucket = 200))
fr <- tree$frame; fr$id <- as.integer(rownames(fr)); fr$leaf <- fr$var == "<leaf>"
leaves_ <- fr[fr$leaf, ]
fi <- read.csv(file.path("..", "analysis", "out", "bias_forest_importance.csv"))
fm <- read.csv(file.path("..", "analysis", "out", "bias_forest_metrics.csv"))
```

Every chart so far looks at one factor at a time. A decision tree looks at all of them together: it asks, one
question after another, which factor best separates the prejudiced answers from the others (an answer is
*prejudiced* when it ties the man's origin to a risk, states a negative stereotype, or says unasked that his
origin does not matter: `r pc(100 * mean(TD$prej))` of the `r num(nrow(TD), 0)` judged answers). The questions
are about the AI (who made it, and its size), the family of the man's nationality (the three families of @fig-words, plus Russia and
Romania between two, and the man with no nationality), the situation, the woman's age, and whether the answer
gives him a religion. Each leaf of @fig-tree gives the share of prejudiced answers at the end of its path.

```{r}
#| label: tree-layout
# layout of the tree: leaves spread left to right in rpart's order, a parent above the middle of its children
lab_ <- labels(tree, pretty = 0)
clean_cond <- function(x) {
  if (startsWith(x, "size")) return(if (grepl("<", x)) "small AI (under 6 billion parameters)"
                                     else "larger AI (6 billion parameters or more)")
  v <- sub("^[a-z_]+=", "", x); var <- sub("=.*$", "", x)
  lv <- strsplit(v, ",", fixed = TRUE)[[1]]
  out <- switch(var,
    publisher = paste(lv, collapse = ", "),
    context = if (length(lv) > 5) paste("all but", paste(sub("^C[0-9]+ ", "", CONTEXTS[setdiff(names(CONTEXTS), lv)]),
                                                        collapse = ", "))
              else paste(sub("^C[0-9]+ ", "", CONTEXTS[lv]), collapse = ", "),
    family = if (setequal(lv, setdiff(names(FAM_LAB), "none"))) "any nationality"
             else paste(sub(" \\(.*", "", FAM_LAB[lv]), collapse = ", "),
    age = paste(sub(" years", "", lv), collapse = " or "),
    religion = paste("religion:", lv), v)
  paste0(c(publisher = "made by ", context = "situation: ", family = "man: ", age = "age: ", religion = "")[[var]], out)
}
fr$cond <- c("all judged answers", vapply(lab_[-1], clean_cond, ""))
fr$depth <- floor(log2(fr$id))
fr$x <- NA_real_; fr$x[fr$leaf] <- seq_len(sum(fr$leaf))
for (d in rev(sort(unique(fr$depth[!fr$leaf])))) for (i in which(!fr$leaf & fr$depth == d))
  fr$x[i] <- mean(fr$x[fr$id %in% c(2 * fr$id[i], 2 * fr$id[i] + 1)])
# drawn sideways: the root on the left, one column per level, the leaves stacked on the right
fr$y <- -fr$x; fr$x <- fr$depth
edges_ <- do.call(rbind, lapply(which(fr$id > 1), function(i) {
  p <- which(fr$id == fr$id[i] %/% 2); data.frame(x = fr$x[p], y = fr$y[p], xend = fr$x[i], yend = fr$y[i])
}))
```

::: {#fig-tree fig-pos="H"}

```{=latex}
\begin{howtoread}\textbf{How to read this chart}\par\smallskip
```

**Reading.** Start on the left, with all the judged answers. At each step the answers are split in two by one question (which AI, which situation, which man, which age); each box says which answers went that way, and the share of them that are prejudiced, from blue (few) to red (many).

```{=latex}
\end{howtoread}
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 4.3
ramp_t <- scales::gradient_n_pal(c("#2a78d6", "#d9d6cf", "#d63c2a"))
fr$fill <- ramp_t(pmin(fr$yval / 0.8, 1))
fr$txt <- paste0(vapply(seq_len(nrow(fr)), \(i) paste(strwrap(fr$cond[i], if (fr$leaf[i]) 27 else 21),
                                                       collapse = "\n"), ""), "\n", pc(100 * fr$yval),
                 " · n = ", num(fr$n, 0))
ggplot() +
  geom_segment(data = edges_, aes(x = x, y = y, xend = (x + xend) / 2, yend = y), colour = "#b9b7b1", linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_segment(data = edges_, aes(x = (x + xend) / 2, y = y, xend = (x + xend) / 2, yend = yend), colour = "#b9b7b1",
               linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_segment(data = edges_, aes(x = (x + xend) / 2, y = yend, xend = xend, yend = yend), colour = "#b9b7b1",
               linewidth = 0.5) +
  geom_label(data = fr, aes(x, y, label = txt, fill = pmin(yval, 0.8), fontface = ifelse(leaf, "bold", "plain")),
             family = "Inter", size = 2.1, lineheight = 0.95, label.size = 0, label.r = unit(3, "pt"),
             label.padding = unit(4, "pt"), colour = ifelse(fr$yval > 0.45 | fr$yval < 0.06, "white", INK)) +
  scale_fill_gradientn(colours = c("#2a78d6", "#d9d6cf", "#d63c2a"), limits = c(0, 0.8),
                       breaks = c(0, 0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8), labels = c("0 %", "20 %", "40 %", "60 %", "80 %"),
                       name = "share of prejudiced answers in the box") +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(add = 0.5)) +
  scale_y_continuous(expand = expansion(add = 0.6)) +
  theme_void(base_family = "Inter") +
  theme(legend.position = "bottom", legend.title = element_text(colour = MUTED, size = 7.5),
        legend.text = element_text(colour = MUTED, size = 7), legend.key.height = unit(6, "pt"),
        legend.key.width = unit(34, "pt"))
```

```{=latex}
\begin{whatitshows}
```

**What it shows.** The first question is the size of the AI, then, for the larger ones, the situation and the man: naming a nationality, any nationality, is what tips the answer (details in the box below).

```{=latex}
\end{whatitshows}
```

Decision tree (rpart regression tree; `r num(nrow(TD), 0)` judged answers; boxes of at least 200 answers).
:::

```{=latex}
\begin{keyfinding}\textbf{\large What the tree tells us}\par\smallskip
```

- **Which AI you ask matters most.** The first split is the size of the model: `r pc(100 * fr$yval[fr$id == 2])`
  of prejudiced answers for the small ones, `r pc(100 * fr$yval[fr$id == 3])` for the larger ones.
- **For the small models, the man's nationality does not even come up**; only who post-trained them does
  (NVIDIA's Nemotron more than Google's own Gemma).
- **For the larger models, naming a nationality is what tips the answer.** In a taxi, an isolated street or an
  elevator, `r pc(100 * fr$yval[fr$id == 14])` of the answers about "a man" are prejudiced, against
  `r pc(100 * fr$yval[fr$id == 15])` as soon as he has a nationality, any nationality.
- **In ordinary situations, the family of the man decides**: men the AI describes by their origin get far more
  prejudiced answers than the warm or reserved ones.
- **The religion the AI gives the man never appears**: it goes with the prejudice, it does not decide it.

The tree shows where prejudice concentrates, not why; and what it counts as prejudice is mostly the "his origin
does not matter" reflex, by far the most frequent indicator.

```{=latex}
\end{keyfinding}
```

A single tree is only one way to split the answers. A **random forest**, 400 trees fitted on random parts of
the data with the 24 nationalities themselves instead of their families, measures how much each factor matters
(with only seven models, size and publisher together identify the model, so their two shares should be read
together):
shuffling a factor and seeing how much worse the forest predicts answers it has never seen (@fig-forest). The
forest predicts a prejudiced answer well (ROC AUC `r num(fm$auc, 2)` on a quarter of the answers kept aside;
0.5 would be chance, 1 perfect); a logistic regression reaches `r num(fm$auc_logistic, 2)` and a small neural
network `r num(fm$auc_neural_net, 2)`: with five factors and no hidden structure, a neural network gains little
and explains less, which is why the report keeps the tree and the forest.

::: {#fig-forest fig-pos="H"}

```{=latex}
\begin{howtoread}\textbf{How to read this chart}\par\smallskip
```

**Reading.** One bar per factor. Its length is how much worse the random forest predicts prejudiced answers when that factor is scrambled: the longer the bar, the more the factor decides whether an answer is prejudiced.

```{=latex}
\end{howtoread}
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 2.2
#| out-width: "80%"
FLAB <- c(size = "the size of the AI", publisher = "who made the AI", context = "the situation", nationality = "the man's nationality",
          age = "the woman's age", religion = "a religion given to him")
fi |> mutate(lab = factor(FLAB[factor], levels = rev(FLAB[fi$factor]))) |>
  ggplot(aes(auc_drop, lab)) +
  geom_col(fill = "#6250d6", width = 0.6) +
  geom_errorbarh(aes(xmin = pmax(auc_drop - 2 * sd, 0), xmax = auc_drop + 2 * sd), height = 0.2, colour = INK) +
  geom_text(aes(label = num(auc_drop, 3)), hjust = -0.3, family = "Inter", size = 2.6, colour = MUTED) +
  scale_x_continuous(expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.15))) +
```

```{=latex}
\begin{whatitshows}
```

**What it shows.** The size of the AI matters most: larger models give far more prejudiced answers. Then the situation, then the man's nationality, then the woman's age, and only then who made the AI. The religion the AI gives the man adds nothing once the rest is known.

```{=latex}
\end{whatitshows}
```

What decides a prejudiced answer: permutation importance of each factor in a random forest (scikit-learn, 400 trees; held-out quarter of the `r num(fm$n, 0)` judged answers; bars: ± 2 standard deviations over 20 shuffles).
:::

**Where are the hot spots?** The tree groups the answers into large boxes. @tbl-hot goes down to finer cells:
the combinations of a model and a nationality, and of a nationality and a situation, with the most prejudiced
answers. The cells are ranked by the lower bound of their 95 % interval, so that a high but uncertain share does
not come first; a model, a nationality and a situation together give only 9 judged answers, too few to rank.

```{r}
#| label: tbl-hot
#| tbl-cap: "The hot spots of prejudice: the ten cells with the highest share of prejudiced answers, ranked by the lower bound of the 95 % Wilson interval. Left: model × nationality (about 99 judged answers per cell). Right: nationality × situation, the seven models pooled (about 63 per cell)."
hot_rank <- function(df, ...) df |> group_by(...) |>
  summarise(k = sum(prej), n = n(), .groups = "drop") |>
  mutate(p = k / n, lo = wilson(k, n)[, "lo"], hi = wilson(k, n)[, "hi"]) |> arrange(desc(lo)) |> head(10)
h1 <- hot_rank(TD |> filter(country != "BASE"), model, country) |>
  transmute(`Model × nationality` = paste(SHORT[model], nm(country), sep = " · "),
            `Prejudiced (95 % interval)` = paste0(pc(100 * p), " (", num(100 * lo, 0), "–", num(100 * hi, 0), ")"))
h2 <- hot_rank(TD |> filter(country != "BASE"), country, context_id) |>
  transmute(`Nationality × situation` = paste(nm(country), sub("^C[0-9]+ ", "", CONTEXTS[context_id]), sep = " · "),
            `Prejudiced (95 % interval) ` = paste0(pc(100 * p), " (", num(100 * lo, 0), "–", num(100 * hi, 0), ")"))
bind_cols(h1, h2) |> kable(booktabs = TRUE, align = "lrlr")
```

The two rankings tell different stories. Between models and nationalities, the hot spots are the men singled out
everywhere in this report: Indian, Afghan, Nigerian and Algerian men, with Granite, Qwen and Gemma 26B. Between
nationalities and situations, almost every cell is the isolated street, whatever the man, Swiss, Finnish or
Japanese included: there, the situation outweighs the nationality, and the AI says that his origin does not
matter for nearly everyone.

## The worst answers

```{r}
#| label: worst-setup
source("R/worst.R")
source("R/translations_key.R")
W <- score_answers(N)
```

Rates hide what the biased answers actually say. This section quotes the most biased answers of each model,
ranked by severity: an association between the man's origin and a risk (the judge's strongest flag) first,
then a negative stereotype, then a defensive marking ("his origin does not matter"); the alarm score breaks
ties. An answer is kept only if the passage behind its flag is found in the text, and that passage is shown
in **bold** at the centre of the excerpt. Answers flagged only for a high alarm are left out, since caution can
be legitimate. Each excerpt is given in the original French, followed by my English translation. **These are model
outputs, not claims.** The same ranking applied context by context, with three answers per model in each
of the eleven contexts, is given in the appendix.

```{r}
#| label: worst-top
#| results: asis
for (m in names(MODELS)) {
  cat("\n\n### ", LAB[[m]], " {.unnumbered}\n\n", sep = "")
  top <- pick_varied(W |> filter(model == m), 3)
  for (i in seq_len(nrow(top))) cat(entry_md(top[i, ], translate = TRUE))
}
```

The worst answers of the three Gemma models and of Nemotron are mild: their few associations are generic
warnings about romance scams, and the other excerpts only say that the man's origin does not matter. Gemma
E2B's refusals do not appear here, since a refusal quotes nothing; they are the subject of @sec-refusals.
Ministral's are the most explicit of the seven models: it attributes scams and trafficking to Albanian and
Nigerian men, and recalls a "media reputation" of violence for Serbian men before adding that most of them
are ordinary citizens.

# Discussion

The results fit in two layers (@fig-layers): one shared by every model, one specific to each.

::: {#fig-layers}

```{=latex}
\begin{howtoread}\textbf{How to read this chart}\par\smallskip
```

**Reading.** Two layers, one above the other. Top: each nationality's share of answers with a cultural compliment, one thin line per AI, nationalities sorted from the most to the least complimented. Bottom: for the men the AIs describe by their origin (Afghanistan, Nigeria, the Maghreb, the Balkans, India…), what each AI does with them: says that his origin does not matter, links him to a risk, or refuses to help.

```{=latex}
\end{howtoread}
```

```{r}
#| fig-height: 5.6
# layer 1: compliments, one line per model
l1 <- sp |> filter(country != "BASE") |>
  mutate(lab = factor(nm(country), levels = nm(sp |> filter(country != "BASE") |> group_by(country) |>
                                                 summarise(m = mean(pct), .groups = "drop") |> arrange(-m) |> pull(country))))
rho_pos <- range(cor(spw_[names(MODELS)], method = "spearman")[upper.tri(diag(NM))])
p1 <- ggplot(l1, aes(lab, pct, group = model, colour = model)) +
  geom_line(linewidth = 0.55, alpha = 0.75) +
  scale_colour_manual(values = COL, guide = "none") +
  scale_y_continuous(labels = \(x) paste0(x, " %")) +
  labs(x = NULL, y = "compliments",
       title = "LAYER 1   What they learnt: who gets the compliments",
       subtitle = sprintf("the seven lines move together: the AIs agree (Spearman ρ from %.2f to %.2f between every pair)",
                          rho_pos[1], rho_pos[2])) +
  theme(axis.text.x = element_text(angle = 45, hjust = 1, vjust = 1, size = 7),
        plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9.5, colour = "#2a78d6"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 7.5, colour = MUTED), panel.grid.major.x = element_blank())
# layer 2: what each model does with the men of the "origin and risk" family
orig_ <- names(fam_of)[fam_of == "origin"]
l2 <- bind_rows(
  D |> filter(country %in% orig_) |> group_by(model) |>
    summarise(`says his origin does not matter` = 100 * mean(defensive_marking),
              `links him to a risk` = 100 * mean(negative_association), .groups = "drop"),
  R |> filter(country %in% orig_) |> group_by(model) |>
    summarise(`refuses to help` = 100 * mean(refusal), .groups = "drop")) |>
  group_by(model) |> summarise(across(everything(), \(x) sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)), .groups = "drop") |>
  pivot_longer(-model, names_to = "what", values_to = "pct") |>
  mutate(mod = factor(SHORT[model], levels = rev(SHORT)),
         what = factor(what, levels = c("says his origin does not matter", "links him to a risk", "refuses to help")))
p2 <- ggplot(l2, aes(pct, mod, fill = what)) +
  geom_col(position = position_dodge(width = 0.8), width = 0.75) +
  scale_fill_manual(values = c("says his origin does not matter" = "#eb6834", "links him to a risk" = "#b4232a",
                               "refuses to help" = "#6250d6"), name = NULL) +
  scale_x_continuous(labels = \(x) paste0(x, " %"), expand = expansion(mult = c(0, 0.05))) +
  labs(x = "share of answers about Afghan, Nigerian, Maghrebi, Balkan, Indian… men", y = NULL,
       title = "LAYER 2   How each was aligned: what it does with the men it does not flatter",
       subtitle = "each AI its own reflex: defend him, name a risk, refuse to help, or say little") +
  theme(plot.title = element_text(face = "bold", size = 9.5, colour = "#d63c2a"),
        plot.subtitle = element_text(size = 7.5, colour = MUTED), panel.grid.major.y = element_blank(),
        legend.position = "bottom", axis.title.x = element_text(size = 7.5))
p1 / p2 + plot_layout(heights = c(1, 1.15))
```

```{=latex}
\begin{whatitshows}
```

**What it shows.** The top layer is shared: whatever the AI, the same men are complimented and the same men are not. The bottom layer is not: for the same men, Granite, Qwen, Gemma 26B and Nemotron mostly say that his origin does not matter, Ministral names a risk, Gemma E2B refuses to help, and Gemma E4B does little of any of it. The first layer looks learnt from shared data; the second, a choice made when each model was aligned.

```{=latex}
\end{whatitshows}
```

The two layers of bias, measured: compliments by nationality for each model (top, judged answers), and what each model does with the men of the "origin and risk" family of @fig-words (bottom; refusals counted on all answers, no judge).
:::

**Two layers of bias.** The seven models agree on who deserves a compliment: Northern
Europeans, Japanese, Italians and Australians get cultural praise and ice-breakers, Afghans, Nigerians,
Algerians, Russians and Indians rarely. This is the most robust signal of the study, shared by five labs
and by every model size tested. What the models do for the other nationalities differs. Granite, Qwen,
Gemma 26B and Nemotron answer with a justification ("his origin does not matter") that presupposes a
suspicion the user never expressed, and they aim it at the same men: probably an effect of alignment, the
model guarding against accusations of racism only for the groups it associates with that risk, which
reveals the association itself. Ministral does not hide the association: it names the risk, in one answer
in ten overall and in four for an Afghan or a Nigerian man. Gemma E4B does neither, and differs from the
others mostly by what it leaves out. Gemma E2B, the smallest, refuses to help, and refuses most for the
same men. A model that seems neutral on one indicator can therefore be biased on another; a benchmark
limited to explicit associations would have rated the three Gemma models almost perfect, and a benchmark
limited to a judge's reading would have missed Gemma E2B's refusals, the strongest nationality effect
found for that model.

**What size and post-training add.** The Gemma family holds the training recipe constant. Its three sizes
keep the same unequal compliments, but the register for the other men changes with size: refusal for
E2B, near silence for E4B, defensive marking for 26B, aimed at the same nationalities as Granite and Qwen.
Nemotron reaches the same register as 26B from E4B, through NVIDIA's post-training alone. The
"his origin does not matter" reflex is therefore not a trace of pre-training data but something a model
acquires, with more capacity or more alignment, and both routes point it at the same men. A larger model
also tailors its advice more to the man's origin: its nationality is easier to guess from the masked
answer. Making a model larger did not make it fairer; it changed the form of the bias, from a refusal
the woman can see to a suspicion she may not notice.

**Targeted explicit associations.** Explicit negative associations are not spread at random: they
reproduce specific media stereotypes ("419" fraud for Nigeria, refugees and the treatment of women for
Afghanistan) and appear mostly in the online first-date context, where the model links nationality to the
risk of a scam. The Nigeria · scam signal, observed on Granite and declared before the other runs, is found
again on Qwen and Ministral: it is a confirmatory result.

**Two pipelines, one picture.** The judge-free analysis reaches the same conclusion as the judge, with
no judge, on the same seven models, and on every answer instead of a sample. It also adds a finding
the judge's rubric could not reach: the split of the nationalities into two vocabularies, one of qualities
for Western men, Brazilians and Japanese, one of origin, tradition, religion and protection for the others.
The clustering of the judge's indicators (@fig-clusters) and the classifier's confusions (@fig-confusion)
draw the same line, and both single out Nigeria and Afghanistan. The refusals, counted without a judge
too, are a third reading, and they fall on the same men.

**Relation to the RTS report.** I find the "encounter" versus "distrust" contrast described by RTS. In
most of the models tested it is attenuated: these open models rarely tip into outright alarm for a given
nationality, and the bias becomes visible only with a repeated design and a control. Ministral is closer
to the report's examples: it is the most alarmist model, and its alarm rises most for Nigeria.

# Limitations {#sec-limitations}

- **Seven open models, one of them quantised.** Six have 2 to 9 billion parameters (counting the
  effective size of E2B and E4B); Gemma 26B-A4B is a mixture of experts with 4 billion active parameters,
  run in 4-bit AWQ, so its answers are those of the quantised model, which may differ slightly from the
  original. All run on two T4 GPUs; Llama and dense models above 10 billion parameters remain to be done
  (Gemma 4 31B does not fit). One family (Gemma) and one base model / post-training pair (Gemma E4B,
  Nemotron) are too few to generalise what size and post-training do.
- **Refusals are counted by a rule.** The refusal rule (a short answer that opens by declining) was
  checked by reading the answers of every model, but a refusal phrased otherwise would be missed. The
  judge also rates refusals, as neutral answers: they lower Gemma E2B's rates of every indicator without
  being a sign of fairness.
- **The judge is less reliable on some models.** On Ministral, the judge's defensive marking disagrees
  with the bench's regular expression (`r pc(by_model(rx_nat, MI, "judge"))` against
  `r pc(by_model(rx_nat, MI, "regex"))`, rank correlation `r num(rx_rho[[MI]], 2)` over nationalities), and
  part of its negative associations are generic warnings. These two indicators are read with care for
  Ministral; the other models show no such gap.
- **Leftovers in the judge-free pipeline.** A few words in the shared vocabulary still point to a place or a
  language rather than to a stereotype (*Canada*, *SAMU*, *gendarmerie*); they are visible in
  the notebook and must not be read as bias. The Reinert classification is simplified (one segment size, no
  double classification as in Iramuteq): its themes are robust enough to read, not to count to the decimal.
- **The judge is a language model.** Qwen3-32B-AWQ can be wrong, and it belongs to the same family as
  Qwen3.5-9B (self-preference cannot be ruled out). The rubric has not been validated against a
  human-annotated sample; reading the quotes shows false positives (for instance a sentence reassuring the
  user about refugee taxi drivers labelled as a "migration" association). The `asks_clarification` field
  remains poorly calibrated for Granite (about 70 % of answers), probably because of offers at the end of
  answers; it is not used in the analysis.
- **Sample size.** About 99 judged answers per nationality and model: gaps of 2 to 3 points are noise,
  and analyses by context (about 9 verdicts per cell and model) are exploratory.
- **Imperfect masking.** Greetings in the country's language, some city names, or demonyms misspelt by
  the models escape masking and may steer the judge.
- **Wealth is one variable among several.** The link with GDP per capita (@sec-wealth) is measured over
  24 countries; it survives the continent, but the countries also differ by religion and media coverage, so it
  describes the pattern, not its cause.
- **Protocol.** French prompts only, a single gender configuration (a woman alone with a man), and uniform
  generation parameters rather than each vendor's recommended settings.

# Conclusion

I asked seven freely available AI models the same question, 7,425 times each: a woman is alone with a man,
what should she do? Only one word changed from one question to the next, the man's nationality. That word
changes the answer.

- **The same men are flattered everywhere.** All seven AIs, made by five companies, compliment Finns,
  Italians or Japanese, and rarely Afghans or Nigerians.
- **The others are met with suspicion, in different ways.** Some AIs insist that "his origin does not
  matter" (Granite, Qwen, Gemma 26B, Nemotron); one names the risk outright, scams, migration or the
  treatment of women (Ministral, in up to four answers in ten for an Afghan or a Nigerian man); the smallest
  refuses to help (Gemma E2B). Some give him a religion and tell the woman to cover up.
- **Even a 15-year-old girl is protected unequally.** She is told to protect herself less often when the man
  is Japanese or British than when he is Nigerian or Afghan, and no AI protects her every time.
- **Bigger is not fairer.** Within one family of models, the bias changes form with size; it does not go
  away.
- **It shows even without a judge.** With the nationality hidden, a simple program still guesses it from the
  answer six times more often than chance.

These are not the large commercial chatbots that RTS tested, but open models that anyone can download, and
the same pattern shows up in all of them. Everything behind this report, prompts, answers, verdicts and
code, is public and can be rerun on free GPUs.

Next steps: test Llama and larger models, check the judge and the refusal rule against human readers, and
repeat the study in other languages.

All notebooks and datasets of the project, published under the name *Alone With a Stranger*, are gathered in a
Kaggle collection [@kaggle_collection]; the source of every notebook, of the analysis scripts and of this report
is on GitHub, at [github.com/adriens/kaggle-bench-ai-biasses](https://github.com/adriens/kaggle-bench-ai-biasses). The
generation notebooks, one per model [@kaggle_granite; @kaggle_qwen; @kaggle_gemma_e2b; @kaggle_gemma; @kaggle_gemma_26b;
@kaggle_ministral; @kaggle_nemotron],
record the model revision, vLLM version, seeds and every answer; the judge notebook [@kaggle_judge] records
the rubric, the judge revision and every verdict; the judge-free notebook [@kaggle_guess] recomputes the
classifier and the lexicometry from every answer of every model; the synthesis notebook [@kaggle_synthesis]
also counts the refusals. The answers and `rts-v4` verdicts analysed here are
released under CC0-1.0 [@kaggle_data]. The GDP per capita and income groups of @sec-wealth come from the World Bank's open data, under CC BY 4.0 [@worldbank_gdp; @worldbank_class], and are kept in the repository (`analysis/data/worldbank.csv`). This report is a Quarto document that recomputes every figure,
table and number from that dataset.

# Appendix: the worst answers, context by context {.unnumbered}

For each of the eleven contexts, the answers of each model that tie the man's origin to a risk (a negative
association) or to a negative stereotype, at most three, ranked as in the main text (severity first, distinct
nationalities when possible). Answers that only say that his origin does not matter are not quoted, only
counted: they are many and alike. Excerpts are in the original French; the judge's decisive passage is in
**bold**, followed by my English translation (of the whole excerpt when it is quoted in the main text, of the
bold passage otherwise). **These are model outputs, not claims.**

```{r}
#| label: worst-by-context
#| results: asis
for (cid in names(CONTEXTS)) {
  cat("\n\n## ", CONTEXTS[[cid]], " {.unnumbered}\n\n", sep = "")
  cat("*", md_safe(TR[[cid]]), "*\n\n", sep = "")
  for (m in names(MODELS)) {
    wm_ <- W |> filter(model == m, context_id == cid)
    top <- pick_varied(wm_ |> filter(assoc_ok | stereo_ok), 3)
    n_def <- sum(!(wm_$assoc_ok | wm_$stereo_ok))
    note <- if (n_def > 0) paste0(n_def, if (n_def == 1) " answer only says" else " answers only say",
                                  " that his origin does not matter.") else ""
    if (nrow(top) == 0) {
      cat("**", LAB[[m]], ":** no negative association or stereotype", if (n_def > 0) "; " else ".",
          if (n_def > 0) tolower(substr(note, 1, 1)) else "", if (n_def > 0) substring(note, 2) else "",
          "\n\n", sep = "")
      next
    }
    cat("\n\n### ", LAB[[m]], " {.unnumbered}\n\n", sep = "")
    for (i in seq_len(nrow(top))) cat(entry_md(top[i, ], show_context = FALSE, translate = TRUE))
    if (n_def > 0) cat("*Also: ", note, "*\n\n", sep = "")
  }
}
```
